title: Numbers to Know System Design Quiz

questions.question: In a typical modern application server, which resource usually becomes the bottleneck first?
questions.explanation: Modern app servers ship with plenty of RAM (64-512GB+) and fast networking, so CPU is usually what saturates first under load -- request parsing, serialization, business logic, TLS. Memory and network can become limits, but typically only after you've already maxed out CPU.
options: RAM -- most servers run out of memory before anything else
CPU -- it usually saturates before memory or network do
Network bandwidth -- the network interface card (NIC) is almost always the first ceiling
Disk space -- app servers fill their disks quickly

questions.question: Modern memory-optimized servers can handle terabytes of data in memory.
questions.explanation: Current memory-optimized instances like the Amazon EC2 U7i High Memory can provide up to 24TB of RAM, allowing entire large datasets to be kept in memory for ultra-fast access patterns that were impossible just a few years ago.

questions.question: For a system storing 10 million records at 1KB each (roughly 10GB total), which storage approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: 10 million records at 1KB each equals only 10GB of data. Even accounting for indexes and related data, this easily fits within a single modern database instance without requiring distributed complexity.
options: Single database instance
Distributed database cluster
Multiple cache layers
Microservice architecture

questions.question: How many writes per second can a modern well-tuned PostgreSQL instance handle?
questions.explanation: A well-tuned PostgreSQL instance on modern hardware can handle 10,000-20,000 writes per second. Many engineers underestimate this and add message queues or write-ahead buffers when a single database would handle the load directly.
options: 100-500 writes/sec
1,000-5,000 writes/sec
100,000+ writes/sec with SSD-backed storage

questions.question: Which situation is the clearest signal, based on the article, that a modern Kafka-like message queue may need to scale?
questions.explanation: The article says modern queues can reach up to about 1 million messages per second per broker, but scaling should be considered when throughput nears roughly 800k messages per second per broker. The other options are within the article’s stated normal capabilities: multi-MB messages, sub-5ms latency, and far more than 300GB of broker storage.
options: Storing 300GB of retained messages on a broker
Handling 2MB messages in the queue
Sustaining around 850k messages per second per broker
Seeing 3ms end-to-end latency within a region

questions.question: A service needs to sustain 5,000 simple writes per second. According to the article, this load fits within the capacity of a single well-tuned PostgreSQL instance, so a message queue is not needed just to add write capacity.
questions.explanation: The article puts a well-tuned PostgreSQL instance at 20,000+ simple writes per second, so a 5,000 writes-per-second workload sits well below that ceiling. The 5,000 figure is the workload, not the database's limit. A queue may still be useful for other requirements, such as absorbing spikes beyond the database's capacity, guaranteeing delivery, or decoupling producers from consumers.

questions.question: AWS RDS for PostgreSQL supports up to 64 TB of storage per instance. Purely on storage size, around when should you start seriously considering sharding?
questions.explanation: With ~64 TB available on a single instance, sharding purely for storage size only makes sense as you approach that ceiling -- and in practice you'll usually hit a different limit (write throughput, operational concerns) before raw size forces your hand. Sharding at 1-10 TB is premature and adds real complexity for no benefit.
options: Around 1 TB, to get ahead of the pain
Around 5-10 TB, to leave room for growth
When you're within striking distance of the limit (roughly 40-50 TB), or you hit a different constraint first
Never -- a single instance is always enough

questions.question: Which of these scenarios does NOT, on its own, call for sharding a single relational database?
questions.explanation: A single modern Postgres or MySQL instance stores tens of terabytes and handles 10-20k write TPS, so 2 TB at 3k writes per second fits comfortably on one primary. The other three are reasons to shard: you've outrun one instance's write capacity, outgrown its storage, or the data volume has made backup and recovery operationally impractical. A table that's merely too large to maintain is different -- partitioning it within the same instance usually solves that without sharding.
options: A 2 TB dataset taking about 3k writes per second
Sustained write throughput well beyond what one instance can handle
A dataset that has grown past the single-instance storage limit
Full backups and restores that take many hours to complete

questions.question: Rank these from fastest to slowest typical latency:
questions.explanation: In-memory cache: sub-1ms. SSD database query: 5-30ms. Cross-region API call: 50-150ms. Understanding these orders of magnitude helps you make appropriate architecture decisions about when caching and geographic distribution matter.

questions.question: Which of these is a valid reason to shard a 5TB database?
questions.explanation: At 5TB, you're well under the 64 TiB storage limit of modern databases. However, if your write throughput exceeds what a single instance can handle (typically 10-20k writes/sec), sharding for write scalability is valid. Data size, architecture patterns, and table count aren't relevant at this scale.
options: The data size exceeds single-instance limits
Write throughput exceeds one instance's capacity
You want to use microservices
You have more than 100 tables

questions.question: A Kafka-like queue receives 500,000 messages/second continuously and retains each message for 7 days. Messages are 1 KB and each broker holds 50 TB (decimal units). Ignoring replication, compression, and overhead, how many brokers are needed for storage? Round up to a whole broker.
questions.explanation: The queue receives 0.5 GB/sec, so 7 days of messages occupy 0.5 × 604,800 = 302,400 GB, or 302.4 TB. Dividing by 50 TB per broker gives 6.048; rounding up gives 7 brokers.
options: 2 brokers
4 brokers
7 brokers
12 brokers

questions.question: A modern message queue can accept a write in roughly 1-5ms, fast enough that enqueuing a message can happen inline during a synchronous request rather than needing its own background step.
questions.explanation: Modern high-performance queues accept a write in roughly 1-5ms end-to-end within a region, so the enqueue itself is cheap enough to do inline in a request-response path instead of offloading the hand-off to a background job. Note this is only about the enqueue step: the downstream work a consumer does is still asynchronous, and you still need a separate mechanism (polling, a callback, a websocket) to return that result to the caller. What the low latency buys you is durable delivery and producer/consumer decoupling without a separate async step just to put the message on the queue -- as long as the queue isn't backlogged.

questions.question: An API tier runs on 10 containerized app servers at a steady 75% CPU. A predictable event in 5 seconds will increase traffic by 40%, requests cannot be queued without violating latency, and new containers take 30–60 seconds to become ready. What is the best design response?
questions.explanation: A 40% traffic jump would push the current fleet from 75% CPU to about 105% before new containers are ready. The article notes 30–60 second startup times and CPU as the usual app-server bottleneck, so predictable spikes require pre-scaling or warm capacity rather than purely reactive scaling.
options: Pre-scale before the event or maintain enough warm headroom before traffic arrives
Rely on reactive autoscaling because container startup is fast enough for this spike
Shard the database because CPU above 70% means the database will become the bottleneck
Increase per-instance memory because modern app servers usually hit memory limits before CPU

questions.question: For a Kafka-like queue, watching only broker ingest throughput can miss a scaling need: steadily growing consumer lag can justify scaling consumers even when each broker is well below roughly 800k messages/second.
questions.explanation: The article lists growing consumer lag as a scaling signal separate from broker throughput. Brokers can accept writes comfortably while consumers fall behind, so the scaling need can come from the consumer side even before broker throughput is near its limit.

questions.question: A 400GB dataset requires cache sharding for optimal performance.
questions.explanation: Not necessarily. Modern memory-optimized cache instances can handle up to 1TB of data. A 400GB dataset fits comfortably within a single cache instance, avoiding the complexity of sharding while maintaining excellent performance.
